passage.title: Racing the Rumbling Earth
passage.author: DRC BEACON Assessment Passage
passage.text:
Deep beneath the ground we walk on, giant slabs of rock press tightly against each other along cracks called faults. For years, rough edges lock these rocks in place while stress builds up. When the rock finally snaps and slips, a burst of stored energy races out in all directions. We feel this sudden shaking on the surface as an earthquake. Yet an earthquake does not travel as one single jolt. Instead, it sends out two main waves that move at very different speeds.

The fastest runner in this underground race is the primary wave, or P-wave. Like a sound wave moving through air, a P-wave pushes and pulls solid rock straight forward and back. Because it squeezes rock in a straight line, it travels nearly four miles per second through Earth's crust. Dogs often bark and window glass rattles when this first pulse passes under a town. Still, P-waves rarely knock down walls or crack roads. They feel more like a quick tap on the floor.

Several seconds later, the slower secondary wave, or S-wave, arrives at the same spot. Traveling at roughly half the speed of the first pulse, an S-wave shakes the ground from side to side and up and down like a snapped rope. This rolling motion twists building frames and shifts heavy bridges. Consequently, most bad damage during an earthquake happens after the S-wave hits.

Scientists use the gap between these two waves to build early warning networks. Inside a buried station, a heavy metal weight hangs from a strong spring above a recorder. When the fast P-wave strikes the vault, the outer frame shakes while the heavy hanging weight stays still. Faint ground tremors from the early P-wave, detected miles from a city by buried seismic sensors, are instantly turned into warning alerts by fast computers. Because radio and fiber-optic signals travel at the speed of light, the computer message outruns the slower S-wave.

Even ten to thirty seconds of early warning can save many lives. Automatic switches slow down high-speed trains so they do not derail. Doctors in hospitals pause delicate work, and fire station doors roll open before the frame can jam. While scientists cannot stop faults from slipping, reading the first wave gives towns time to brace for the second.

tier2Words.definition: a single short burst or beat of energy moving through a space
tier2Words.rootHint: Latin root pellere ('to push or beat')
tier2Words.contextClue: When this first burst of wave energy passes under a town, windowpanes rattle before the second wave arrives.

tier2Words.definition: as a result or outcome of what just happened
tier2Words.rootHint: Latin root sequi ('to follow') + prefix con- ('with')
tier2Words.contextClue: Because an S-wave twists building frames and shifts bridges, most serious damage happens as a result.

tier2Words.definition: slight quivering or shaking movements of the ground
tier2Words.rootHint: Latin root tremere ('to shake or tremble')
tier2Words.contextClue: Buried sensors detect the faint shaking caused by the early P-wave before the stronger S-wave arrives.

tier2Words.definition: to run off the metal tracks
tier2Words.rootHint: Prefix de- ('off, away from') + rail ('metal track')
tier2Words.contextClue: Automatic switches slow down high-speed trains before the shaking ground can throw them off the tracks.

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 4:

"Faint ground tremors from the early P-wave, detected miles from a city by buried seismic sensors, are instantly turned into warning alerts by fast computers."

Based on the sentence, what detects the faint ground tremors, and what turns them into warning alerts?

options.text: Fast computers detect the faults underground, and buried seismic sensors send out radio alerts.
options.childFeedback: This swaps the two roles! The buried seismic sensors are what detect the ground tremors, and the fast computers are what turn them into warning alerts.

options.text: Buried seismic sensors detect the faint ground tremors, and fast computers turn them into warning alerts.
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 4, 'detected miles from a city by buried seismic sensors' and 'are instantly turned into warning alerts by fast computers' show that buried sensors detect the tremors and fast computers turn them into alerts.

options.text: The early P-wave turns the buried seismic sensors into fast computers near the city.
options.childFeedback: This scrambles the sentence! An earthquake wave does not turn underground sensors into computers.

options.text: Barking dogs detect the S-wave first, and train drivers phone the fire stations.
options.childFeedback: Barking dogs are mentioned in Paragraph 2, and trains and fire stations are mentioned in Paragraph 5, not in this sentence from Paragraph 4.

questions.provingSentenceText: Faint ground tremors from the early P-wave, detected miles from a city by buried seismic sensors, are instantly turned into warning alerts by fast computers.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 4, 'detected miles from a city by buried seismic sensors' and 'are instantly turned into warning alerts by fast computers' show that buried sensors detect the tremors and fast computers turn them into alerts.
questions.parentExplanation: This passive sentence features two 'by' phrases: 'detected... by buried seismic sensors' and 'are instantly turned into warning alerts by fast computers'. Option B correctly identifies both agents.
questions.retryHint: Check the two 'by' phrases in Paragraph 4: 'detected... by...' and 'are instantly turned into warning alerts by...'

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 4:

"Faint ground tremors from the early P-wave, detected miles from a city by buried seismic sensors, are instantly turned into warning alerts by fast computers."

What does the word tremors mean as it is used in Paragraph 4?

options.text: Deep underground caves filled with water
options.childFeedback: The sensors sit inside a buried station vault in Paragraph 4, not in water-filled caves, and 'tremors' comes from the P-wave shaking the ground.

options.text: Loud sirens mounted on the roofs of fire stations
options.childFeedback: Fire stations are mentioned in Paragraph 5, while 'faint ground tremors from the early P-wave' in Paragraph 4 refers to the shaking of the earth.

options.text: Heavy metal weights that never move at all
options.childFeedback: The hanging metal weight inside the recorder stays still while the outer frame shakes, so 'ground tremors' means the shaking movements, not the still weight.

options.text: Slight shaking or vibrating movements in the earth
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 4, 'tremors' means slight shaking or vibrating movements in the earth, because the buried sensors detect the faint ground shaking caused by the early P-wave.

questions.provingSentenceText: Faint ground tremors from the early P-wave, detected miles from a city by buried seismic sensors, are instantly turned into warning alerts by fast computers.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 4, 'tremors' means slight shaking or vibrating movements in the earth, because the buried sensors detect the faint ground shaking caused by the early P-wave.
questions.parentExplanation: In Paragraph 4, 'faint ground tremors from the early P-wave' refers to the mild shaking vibrations detected by buried seismic sensors.
questions.retryHint: Look at how the fast P-wave shakes the outer frame of the buried station in Paragraph 4 to see what 'ground tremors' are.

questions.prompt: Based on Paragraph 3, why do S-waves cause much more damage to buildings and bridges than P-waves?

options.text: They shake the ground side to side and up and down, which twists building frames.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 3 explains that while a P-wave just squeezes rock in a straight line, an S-wave shakes the ground from side to side and up and down like a snapped rope, which twists building frames and shifts bridges.

options.text: They travel twice as fast as P-waves and arrive before sensors can turn on.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 3 states the exact opposite about speed: the S-wave is the slower wave, traveling at roughly half the speed of the P-wave.

options.text: They cut the fiber-optic cables that connect hospitals to fire stations.
options.childFeedback: Fiber-optic cables are mentioned in Paragraph 4 because they carry light-speed warning alerts, not because S-waves cut them.

options.text: They melt the solid rock deep beneath the fault into hot liquid lava.
options.childFeedback: Neither paragraph mentions melting rock into liquid lava; earthquakes shake solid rock along faults.

questions.provingSentenceText: Traveling at roughly half the speed of the first pulse, an S-wave shakes the ground from side to side and up and down like a snapped rope.
questions.childTip: Paragraph 3 explains that while a P-wave just squeezes rock in a straight line, an S-wave shakes the ground from side to side and up and down like a snapped rope, which twists building frames and shifts bridges.
questions.parentExplanation: Paragraph 3 explains that S-waves shake the ground side to side and up and down like a snapped rope, a rolling motion that twists building frames and shifts heavy bridges.
questions.retryHint: Read the second and third sentences of Paragraph 3 to see how an S-wave moves the ground like a snapped rope.

questions.prompt: How does the author organize the information in Paragraphs 2 and 3?

options.text: By explaining step by step how engineers pour concrete for highway bridges
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 3 mentions that S-waves shift heavy bridges, but neither paragraph explains how engineers pour concrete to build bridges.

options.text: By listing the dates of the ten largest earthquakes in United States history
options.childFeedback: The passage never gives a list of historical earthquake dates; it explains the science of seismic waves and early warning systems.

options.text: By comparing the speed, motion, and impact of P-waves and S-waves
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 2 describes the fast, straight-line P-wave that causes little damage, and Paragraph 3 contrasts it with the slower, rolling S-wave that causes most earthquake damage.

options.text: By arguing that buried seismic sensors are too expensive for small towns to use
options.childFeedback: Seismic sensors are not introduced until Paragraph 4, and the author never argues that they are too expensive for small towns.

questions.provingSentenceText: Several seconds later, the slower secondary wave, or S-wave, arrives at the same spot.
questions.childTip: Paragraph 2 describes the fast, straight-line P-wave that causes little damage, and Paragraph 3 contrasts it with the slower, rolling S-wave that causes most earthquake damage.
questions.parentExplanation: Paragraphs 2 and 3 use a comparison/contrast and sequence structure to contrast the fast, mild, straight-line P-wave with the slower, destructive, rolling S-wave.
questions.retryHint: Compare how Paragraph 2 describes the first wave (P-wave) with how Paragraph 3 describes the second wave (S-wave).

questions.prompt: Part A: Based on the passage, why is an earthquake warning system able to alert a city before the dangerous shaking begins?

options.text: Satellites in space can see underground faults glowing red a full week before an earthquake starts.
options.childFeedback: The passage never mentions space satellites or glowing red faults; Paragraph 5 notes that scientists cannot stop faults from slipping ahead of time.

options.text: Heavy metal weights inside the fault stop the rocks from slipping until trains have come to a full stop.
options.childFeedback: The hanging metal weight is inside a recording station to measure shaking—it cannot hold giant underground rock faults in place.

options.text: S-waves travel much faster than radio signals, giving computers several hours to predict the storm.
options.childFeedback: This reverses the speeds! S-waves are slower than P-waves, and light-speed radio signals are much faster than S-waves, giving ten to thirty seconds of warning.

options.text: Sensors detect the harmless P-wave first and send light-speed computer signals that arrive ahead of the slower S-wave.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 4 explains that buried sensors detect the fast, mostly harmless P-wave first and computers send radio and fiber-optic alerts at the speed of light, outrunning the slower, damaging S-wave.

questions.provingSentenceText: Because radio and fiber-optic signals travel at the speed of light, the computer message outruns the slower S-wave.
questions.childTip: Paragraph 4 explains that buried sensors detect the fast, mostly harmless P-wave first and computers send radio and fiber-optic alerts at the speed of light, outrunning the slower, damaging S-wave.
questions.parentExplanation: Paragraph 4 explains that buried sensors detect the fast P-wave first, and because radio and fiber-optic signals move at the speed of light, the warning alert outruns the slower, destructive S-wave.
questions.retryHint: Look at the last two sentences of Paragraph 4 to see how the computer alert races ahead of the slower S-wave.
